name: Lighting Rigs and Relighting
title: Lighting Rigs and Relighting
answer: Lighting rigs and relighting in AI image generation cover the placement, color, intensity, and falloff of virtual lights, and the process of changing the illumination in an existing photograph or render. In hyper-real photography this means matching studio strobes, softboxes, and practical lights so that synthetic subjects sit believably in a scene. Relighting also covers reflections, shadows, and ambient occlusion, not just direct light. Working photographers use these controls for product shots, portrait retouching, and pre-visualizing film or advertising setups.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Relighting models run on the same GPU infrastructure as other generative image systems, typically diffusion or consistency models fine-tuned for lighting conditioning. They require high-memory graphics cards for local use or cloud APIs for batch work, and often pair a base image with a depth map, normal map, or segmentation mask. Among the 1000 live image generation models this site tracks, a growing subset exposes explicit lighting rig parameters rather than treating light as an implicit prompt detail.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work usually starts with either a 3D scene where the artist places virtual lights, or a flat image where the model estimates surface orientation and existing shading. The system then separates color from illumination, applies the new light rig, and recombines them so that highlights, shadows, and reflections stay consistent. Artists iterate by adjusting light position, temperature, and softness, often using HDR environment maps or simple directional, point, and area lights. The goal is not just brighter or darker pixels but a physically plausible change in how materials respond.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Relighting raises provenance concerns because it can change the apparent time of day, location, or mood of a photo without leaving obvious edits. Portraits and documentary images are especially sensitive, since altered lighting can imply consent to a setting that never existed. Rights questions also follow the training data, as models learn lighting from copyrighted photographs and renders. Provenance tools that record edit steps are becoming part of professional workflow, though they are not yet universal.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Relighting is moving from still images to video, where the challenge is keeping light and shadows stable across frames. As the site's count of 1000 video models grows, expect more tools that relight a clip from a single reference frame or text description. On-device relighting for phone cameras and real-time previews in viewfinders are also likely, along with better handling of transparent and translucent materials.
